what_its_for: Oxaprozin is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve pain, swelling, and stiffness caused by arthritis, including osteoarthritis (wear-and-tear arthritis) and rheumatoid arthritis. It works by reducing the chemicals in your body that cause pain and inflammation.
how_to_take: Take oxaprozin by mouth, usually once a day, with a full glass of water. You may take it with food, milk, or an antacid if it upsets your stomach. Do not lie down for at least 10 minutes after taking this medicine. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush or chew it. Take this medicine at the same time each day to help you remember.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 1200 mg (two 600 mg tablets) taken once a day. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose (600 mg once daily) or adjust your dose based on your condition and how well you respond to the medicine. Do not take more than 1800 mg per day or more than 26 mg per kg of body weight per day, whichever is less. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If it is the next day or almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose as normal. Do not double up or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store oxaprozin at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program near you.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking oxaprozin, as it increases your risk of stomach bleeding. Do not take other NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin for pain) at the same time unless your doctor tells you to. Avoid taking this medicine if you are pregnant, especially in the third trimester (last 3 months), as it can harm the unborn baby. Be careful when driving or using machinery, as this medicine can occasionally cause dizziness. Avoid prolonged sun exposure as oxaprozin can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight — use sunscreen and wear protective clothing when outdoors.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: black, tarry, or bloody stools; vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds; severe stomach pain; chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or slurred speech (signs of a heart attack or stroke); swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; skin rash, blisters, or peeling; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine or decreased urination; unusual weight gain or swelling in your legs or feet; or vision changes. Also call your doctor if your pain or swelling does not improve or gets worse.
when_it_works: Some people notice a little relief from pain within a few days of starting oxaprozin. However, it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use to feel the full benefit for arthritis symptoms. Keep taking it as directed even if you do not feel immediate results. Let your doctor know if you do not see improvement after 2 weeks.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): You may be at higher risk for stomach bleeding, kidney problems, and heart-related side effects. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose and monitor you more closely. Children: Oxaprozin is sometimes used in children ages 6 to 16 years with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, but the dose is based on body weight and must be carefully determined by your doctor. Kidney or liver disease: Use with caution. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or choose a different medicine. Pregnancy: Avoid use, especially during the last 3 months of pregnancy, as it can cause serious harm to the unborn baby. Talk to your doctor right away if you become pregnant while taking this medicine. Breastfeeding: It is not fully known whether oxaprozin passes into breast milk. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor before breastfeeding.
